CT561 Paper-Based Topic Guide

Supporting Structures: Delays, Smoothing, Little's Law and Behaviour

These are lower-frequency than the four main question families, but they recur often enough to prepare as short-question and extension material.

Paper-backed question forms

  • Smoothing [8]: show the stock-flow structure that converts a noisy input into a smoothed signal and explain adjustment time. 2023/24 Q2(a)
  • Little's Law [3-7]: calculate average delay from stock and throughput, state equilibrium conditions and infer delay distribution. 2017/18 Q4(a,b); 2018/19 Q1(c)
  • Behaviour to structure [8]: infer a one-stock reinforcing or balancing structure from a graph. 2023/24 Q1(a)
  • Analytical/differential model [8]: convert a differential equation to stock-flow form and explain its feedback. 2016/17 Q2(b); 2017/18 Q2(a); 2021/22 Q2(a)

Smoothing with a first-order delay [8]

For input V and smoothed output V Smooth, draw a stock V Smooth with an adjustment flow from the discrepancy:

V Smooth = INTEG((V - V Smooth)/Adjustment Time, Initial Smooth)

A larger adjustment time makes the output smoother but slower to react. A smaller adjustment time tracks the input more closely. This is a balancing goal-seeking structure, not an arithmetic average of the most recent fixed number of observations.

Little's Law [3-7]

Average Stock = Average Throughput x Average Delay
Average Delay = Average Stock / Average Throughput

For the broadband example: 5,000 installations / 2,500 installations per month = 2 months. It applies to averages in a stable system, where average inflow equals average outflow. It does not mean every customer waits exactly two months.

In 2018/19, the steady state delay was found as 6 from stock/throughput. When the outflow resembles a delayed and smoothed version of inflow, it suggests a distributed delay rather than every item taking one fixed delay.

Recognising one-stock behaviour [8]

  • Increasing at an increasing rate: likely reinforcing growth, for example Stock = INTEG(Fractional Increase x Stock, Initial).
  • Rising then flattening towards a limit: likely balancing feedback, for example a goal-seeking or carrying-capacity structure.
  • Inflection point: the stock changes from increasing slope to decreasing slope, or vice versa. It indicates a maximum/minimum in the net flow, not necessarily a maximum/minimum in stock.

Differential equation to a model [8]

For dS/dt = t, draw one stock S with an inflow t and use the Vensim time variable. With S(0)=0, analytical integration gives S(t)=t^2/2, so S(20)=200. For Euler questions, use the stated DT instead of the analytical result.

For logistic growth, separate the positive and negative terms into flows so that the balancing carrying-capacity effect is visible.

Mark checklist

  • State the conditions under which a formula applies.
  • For a graph, name the behaviour and the likely feedback structure.
  • For a delay/smoothing structure, say what adjustment time changes.
  • Keep this topic secondary to integration, feedback, SIR and stock management when allocating revision time.
